transcript.text: So if I'm trying to get my wife to go to
the restaurant that I want to go to
dinner, like what do I say? So a dummy
might say, "Hey babe, want to go to
Cheesecake Factory?" And she might be
like, "Well, no, I don't want to go to
Cheesecake Factory." Or well, you know,
"I'm not really sure." Now a smart
person might say, "Babe, would you be
against going to Cheesecake Factory, one
of the finest dining establishments in
the land?" And she's like, "Well, I'm
not against going to Cheesecake
Factory." And I'm like, "Great, well
then let's go." And that's the beauty of
a no base question. See how different
it's phrased, how different it feels? A
sales example would be like, "Hey, are
you excited to move forward today?" It's
harder to get someone to say, "Yes, I'm
excited to move forward today." So
instead just say, "Would you be opposed
to moving forward at the end of this
conversation?" Or "Would we be crazy if
we got you signed up?" It's easier to
get someone to say, "No, I'm not
opposed." Or "No, it wouldn't be crazy."
And great, now we got the sale. The
psychology behind this is that people
feel safer saying no. And so people like
to feel that they retain their autonomy
in decision making. They feel like
they're at ease when they say no. And at
the end of the day, people don't want to
be responsible for anything. And they
don't want to feel vulnerable to saying
yes or agreeing to something, right? So
instead, they prefer to say no and stay
safe. But if you phrase your questions
properly, you can get people to say yes
by saying no, which is one of the most
powerful sales tactics out there. Now to
be clear, you're not going to get
someone to buy a house by saying, "You
wouldn't be opposed to buying this
house?" No, this is a nudge, not a
massive sledgehammer.
